newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Killing of Cambodian PM's relative "political".
newsitem.headline: Killing of Cambodian PM's relative "political".

text.p: The brother-in-law of co-Premier Hun Sen was shot dead on Tuesday morning in what one offical described as a politically motivated attack.
Om Yentieng, a spokesman for Hun Sen, said: "This is a political murder," adding that the second prime minister had cancelled his official schedule on Tuesday.

A tearful Hun Sen said the killing was meant as a warning to Khmer Rouge separatists who, in a press conference at his house on Saturday, spoke out against a leading opposition party and Hun Sen's coalition partner, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
"This is a threat to Khmer Rouge separatists to show them that even the life of the brother of Hun Sen could not be protected, so how could their own lives be protected," Hun Sen said.
"They threaten the Khmer Rouge through my brother's murder," he added in an address from his home shown on state television.
Keov Savuth, 39, was shot in the chest three times as he left a restaurant at 8:35 a.m. (0135 GMT), said a restaurant worker who witnessed the murder.
Hun Sen said he would use military force if necessary to protect the separatists from his brother-in-law's assassins.
"I try to keep peace, but I also have the ability to order the army to fight in a few hours or in a few days if it is necessary to protect the lives of the people," he said.
Keov Savuth's widow, Lim Sotha, said at a wake where his shrouded body was lying that one man fired six shots and hit with five after waiting at the restaurant with a gun hidden under his paper.
Keov Savuth, who was married to Hun Sen's wife's sister and was employed as a senior Interior Ministry police official, died soon after arriving at a Phnom Penh hospital, officials said.
Om Yentieng said he believed he himself was also under threat. He said Hun Sen had sent security guards to watch him and any other possible targets for assassination.
"This is not the first time that Hun Sen's family has been targetted," he said, citing the 1992 murder of his father-in-law.
The event brings political tensions in Phnom Penh to a head.

At the weekend, 10 Cambodians who said they had been undercover Khmer Rouge agents accused opposition leader and former finance minister Sam Rainsy of taking secret funds and support from the pariah Maoist movement. Sam Rainsy advocates reconciliation with the Khmer Rouge.
The men, who said they were defecting Khmer Rouge spies from Phnom Penh, met Hun Sen on Saturday.

The self-proclaimed guerrillas said they had given support and funding to an opposition party since co-Premiers Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
Ranariddh called the men liars and Sam Rainsy said he had been slandered.
An adviser to Ranariddh told Reuters: "The prince has condemned this act very severely on behalf of (his) FUNCINPEC party."
An investigation had begun and three witnesses were being interviewed, officials said.
Hun Sen appealed to the killers to reveal themselves and said he would allow them to go free if they would identify the people who ordered the murder.
